claim: The Western honeybee (Apis mellifera) can keep the brood area constantly at 34 °C.
source: The Western honeybee (Apis mellifera) owns incredible thermoregulation strategies, which allow the colony to keep the brood area constantly at 34 °C (Simpson, 1961).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Simpson, 1961.

claim: Honeybee thermoregulation contributes to their almost worldwide distribution.
source: Due to this special feature, honeybees are relatively independent of the ambient temperature (TA), which may contribute decisively to their almost worldwide distribution (Wallberg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wallberg et al., 2014.

claim: Honeybee thermoregulation includes thermogenesis.
source: In contrast to other ectotherms, honeybee thermoregulation includes thermogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of honeybees compared to other ectotherms, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Worker bees actively increase their thorax temperatures.
source: Here, primarily workerbees actively increase their thorax temperatures (TTHX, Kovac et al., 2009; Stabentheiner et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kovac et al., 2009 and Stabentheiner et al., 2010.

claim: Thermogenesis enables foraging at ambient temperatures below 10 °C.
source: This thermogenesis is of immense social importance, because it enables foraging at TA below 10 °C (Bujok et al., 2002; Stabentheiner et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bujok et al., 2002 and Stabentheiner et al., 2003.

claim: Thermogenesis enables proper brood development.
source: This thermogenesis is of immense social importance, because it enables foraging at TA below 10 °C (Bujok et al., 2002; Stabentheiner et al., 2003) and a proper brood development (Himmer, 1932; Weiss, 1962; Tautz et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Himmer, 1932; Weiss, 1962; Tautz et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Thermogenesis reduces parasite infections.
source: reduces parasite infections (Starks et al., 2000; Campbell et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Starks et al., 2000 and Campbell et al., 2010.

claim: Thermogenesis is a powerful defense mechanism against predatory hornets.
source: and is a powerful defense mechanism against predatory hornets (Ken et al., 2005; Baracchi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ken et al., 2005 and Baracchi et al., 2010.

claim: The individual heating pattern of worker bees consists of a wave-like rise and fall in thorax temperature.
source: The individual heating pattern of workerbees consists of a wave-like rise and fall in TTHX (Kronenberg and Heller, 1982)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kronenberg and Heller, 1982.

claim: Honeybee thermogenesis is realized exclusively by the activation of the indirect flight muscles.
source: and is realized exclusively by the activation of the indirect flight muscles, formed by the dorsoventral wing elevators (DV) and the dorsal-longitudinal wing depressors (DL), even if wing and thorax vibration are not visible (Esch et al., 1991; Esch and Goller, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Esch et al., 1991 and Esch and Goller, 1991.

claim: Flight muscles are utilized in flight, fanning, and communication during the waggle dance.
source: However, these muscles are utilized in various other behaviors, which includes flight (Esch et al., 1975; Esch, 1976), fanning (Simpson, 1961) and communication during the waggle dance (Esch, 1961; Wenner, 1962).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Esch et al., 1975; Esch, 1976; Simpson, 1961; Esch, 1961; Wenner, 1962.

claim: Diverse contraction mechanisms exist for flight muscles which must be controlled differently.
source: In order to perform these various tasks, diverse contraction mechanisms exist which must be controlled differently (Esch and Goller, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Esch and Goller, 1991.

claim: Octopamine has a crucial role in insect flight muscles.
source: Some evidence indicates a crucial role of octopamine in the insect flight muscles (Blau and Wegener, 1994; Blau et al., 1994; Wegener, 1996; Duch et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blau and Wegener, 1994; Blau et al., 1994; Wegener, 1996; Duch et al., 1999.

claim: It remains unknown whether octopamine is used as a neurochemical in honeybee flight muscles.
source: Unfortunately, it remains unknown whether octopamine is used as a neurochemical in honeybee flight muscles or whether an octopamine receptor gene is expressed in these tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: DV and DL are under control of the mesometa-thoracic ganglion (MMTG).
source: However, DL and DV are under control of the mesometa-thoracic ganglion (MMTG, Markl, 1966)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Markl, 1966.

claim: Octopaminergic innervation of the flight muscles seems to be a conserved feature in insects.
source: and the octopaminergic innervation of the flight muscles seems to be a conserved feature in insects (Duch et al., 1999; Schlurmann and Hausen, 2003; Pauls et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duch et al., 1999; Schlurmann and Hausen, 2003; Pauls et al., 2018.

claim: The brain octopamine concentration of worker bees is significantly decreased due to cold stress.
source: It was further demonstrated that the brain octopamine concentration of workerbees is significantly decreased due to cold stress (Chen et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2008.

claim: Honeybee β octopamine receptor genes (AmOARβ1-3/4) are subject to altitudinal adaptation processes.
source: In this context, Wallberg et al., 2017 made the observation that honeybee β octopamine receptor genes (AmOARβ1-3/4) are subject to altitudinal adaptation processes in honeybees.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wallberg et al., 2017.

claim: Octopamine and dopamine are detectable in both DV and DL.
source: We can detect octopamine and dopamine in both, DV and DL, whereas serotonin and tyramine are not detectable (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Serotonin and tyramine are not detectable in DV and DL.
source: We can detect octopamine and dopamine in both, DV and DL, whereas serotonin and tyramine are not detectable (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Newly emerged bees which cannot perform thermogenesis have the lowest octopamine concentration in DV and DL.
source: Newly emerged bees which cannot perform thermogenesis have the lowest octopamine concentration in DV and DL (Figure 1A–B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The octopamine concentration increases with the age of the worker bee in DV and DL.
source: and the octopamine concentration increases with the age of the workerbee (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The concentrations of dopamine have a different time course in DV and DL compared to octopamine.
source: In contrast to octopamine, the concentrations of dopamine have a different time course in DV and DL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Octopamine, serotonin, dopamine, and tyramine are detectable in the MMTG.
source: In addition to octopamine, serotonin, dopamine, and tyramine are also detectable, but no age-related differences can be observed for any of these monoamines (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: No age-related differences can be observed for monoamines in the MMTG.
source: In addition to octopamine, serotonin, dopamine, and tyramine are also detectable, but no age-related differences can be observed for any of these monoamines (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Octopamine-like immunoreactivity is observable in four individual cell clusters in the MMTG.
source: Octopamine-like immunoreactivity (OA-IR) is observable in four individual cell clusters, with most of the cell bodies being found at the ventral midline (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: Most octopamine-like immunoreactive cell bodies are found at the ventral midline of the MMTG.
source: Octopamine-like immunoreactivity (OA-IR) is observable in four individual cell clusters, with most of the cell bodies being found at the ventral midline (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: Some octopamine-like immunoreactive cell bodies are located at the dorsal midline of the MMTG.
source: Some OA-IR positive cell bodies are also located at the dorsal midline (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Most MMTG leaving nerves show octopamine-like immunoreactivity.
source: Most MMTG leaving nerves show OA-IR (Figure 2G–I), as varicose fibers in IIN1 and a thicker axonal bundle in IIN3 demonstrate (Figure 2G1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Finest octopamine-like immunoreactive varicose structures can be found directly at muscle fibers.
source: Finally, finest OA-IR positive varicose structures can be found directly at muscle fibers (Figure 2J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J-K.

claim: Strong signals for PCR products for AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2 are observed in flight muscles.
source: We observe strong signals for PCR products for AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2, weak DNA bands for AmOARβ1 and AmOARβ3/4, and no amplification product in the case of AmOARα2 and both tyramine receptor genes (AmTAR1 & AmTAR2; Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Weak DNA bands for AmOARβ1 and AmOARβ3/4 are observed in flight muscles.
source: We observe strong signals for PCR products for AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2, weak DNA bands for AmOARβ1 and AmOARβ3/4, and no amplification product in the case of AmOARα2 and both tyramine receptor genes (AmTAR1 & AmTAR2; Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No amplification product for AmOARα2 and both tyramine receptor genes (AmTAR1 & AmTAR2) is observed in flight muscles.
source: We observe strong signals for PCR products for AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2, weak DNA bands for AmOARβ1 and AmOARβ3/4, and no amplification product in the case of AmOARα2 and both tyramine receptor genes (AmTAR1 & AmTAR2; Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PCR products indicate the expression for all known honeybee octopamine and tyramine receptor genes in neural tissues (brain, MMTG).
source: In addition, PCR products indicate the expression for all known honeybee octopamine and tyramine receptor genes in neural tissues (brain, MMTG).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PCR analysis.

claim: AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2 expression can be observed in DV and DL in all age groups of worker bees.
source: AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2 expression can be observed in DV and DL in all age groups of workerbees.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR analysis.

claim: Relative expression of AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2 increases with age in flight muscles.
source: Here, relative expression increases with age, as shown by significant differences between newly emerged bees (0 days) and the three oldest groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR analysis showing significant differences.

claim: Reserpine depletes octopamine in the flight muscles.
source: This drug has the ability to deplete vesicles on monoaminergic synapses (Plummer et al., 1954; Cheung and Parmar, 2020). The octopamine concentrations in DV and DL are significantly decreased due to our treatment (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B and citations to Plummer et al., 1954 and Cheung and Parmar, 2020.

claim: Reserpine does not affect dopamine concentration in the flight muscle.
source: In contrast, the dopamine concentration in the flight muscle seems not to be affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reserpine does not affect octopamine concentrations in the MMTG.
source: The same is true for the concentrations of octopamine (Figure 4C) and of the other monoamines in the MMTG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reserpinized bees show hypothermia when compared with control.
source: The reserpine feeding additionally causes hypothermia in both, nurse bees and forager bees (Figure 4D, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Table 3.

claim: Injection of octopamine into the flight muscles reverses reserpine-induced hypothermia.
source: We reversed the reserpine-induced hypothermia by injecting octopamine directly into the flight muscles (Figure 4, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Table 3.

claim: Octopamine signaling is necessary for honeybee thermogenesis.
source: Thus, we conclude that octopamine signaling in the flight muscles is necessary for thermogenesis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the reserpine depletion and octopamine rescue experiments.

claim: β octopamine receptors are positively coupled to membrane-bound adenylyl cyclases (mAC).
source: Via Gαs proteins, these receptors are positively coupled to membrane-bound adenylyl cyclases (mAC), which leads to an increase of the intracellular adenosine 3',5'-cyclic mono-phosphate (cAMP) concentration upon receptor activation (Balfanz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Balfanz et al., 2014.

claim: Tissue cAMP concentration is significantly lower in reserpinized bees when compared with control.
source: The tissue cAMP concentration is significant lower in reserpinized bees when compared with control (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D (likely referring to Figure 4F based on the figure content).

claim: Octopamine injection into the flight muscles of reserpinized bees leads to a strong increase of the tissue cAMP concentration.
source: Furthermore, octopamine injection into the flight muscles of reserpinized bees leads to a strong increase of the tissue cAMP concentration (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D (likely referring to Figure 4F based on the figure content).

claim: Tissue cGMP concentrations are not affected by reserpine treatment.
source: The tissue guanosine 3',5'-cyclic monophosphate (cGMP) concentrations seem not to be affected by our treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mianserin leads to hypothermia in nurse bees and forager bees.
source: The non-selective but potent octopamine receptor antagonist mianserin leads to hypothermia (Figure 5A, Table 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Table 3.

claim: Yohimbine does not cause hypothermia.
source: while the effective tyramine receptor and α octopamine receptor antagonist yohimbine does not (Figure 5B, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Table 3.

claim: Alprenolol causes hypothermia.
source: Finally, alprenolol causes hypothermia too (Figure 5C, Table 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Table 3.

claim: Carvedilol and metoprolol did not have an observable effect on thermogenesis.
source: whereas carvedilol and metoprolol did not have an observable effect on thermogenesis (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: Rp-8-CPT-cAMPS negatively affects thermogenesis in both nurse bees and forager bees.
source: Rp-8-CPT-cAMPS negatively effects thermogenesis in both, nurse bees and forager bees (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pyruvate concentrations increase significantly after octopamine stimulation.
source: Pyruvate concentrations increase significantly after octopamine stimulation (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: AmGAPDH gene shows increased expression triggered by cold stress.
source: Finally, we observed that the AmGAPDH gene shows increased expression triggered by cold stress (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: AmGAPDH expression can be increased by octopamine injection into the flight muscles.
source: A similar increase in AmGAPDH expression can be observed when the bees were treated with an octopamine injection in to the flight muscles instead of cold stress. (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Octopamine is present in workerbee flight muscles.
source: We can demonstrate that octopamine is present in workerbee flight muscles by independent analysis methods (HPLC-ECD, antibody labeling).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from HPLC-ECD and antibody labeling.

claim: Octopamine in flight muscles is most likely delivered via flight muscle innervating neurons from the MMTG.
source: This is most likely delivered via flight muscle innervating neurons from the MMTG.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical and immunohistochemical data.

claim: The honeybee MMTG is formed by fusion of four neuromers (mesothorax, metathorax, first and second abdominal ganglia).
source: The honeybee MMTG is formed by fusion of four neuromers (mesothorax, methathorax, first and second abdominal ganglia; Markl, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Markl, 1966.

claim: The MMTG nerves IIN1 and IIN3 innervate DV and DL, respectively.
source: Furthermore, the MMTG nerves IIN1 and IIN3 innervate DV and DL, respectively (Markl, 1966; Pan, 1980)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Markl, 1966 and Pan, 1980.

claim: Octopaminergic neurons from the MMTG directly innervate the flight muscles.
source: We conclude, that octopaminergic neurons from the MMTG directly innervate the flight muscles and therefore influence thermogenesis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the immunohistochemical and anatomical data.

claim: Newly emerged bees cannot perform thermogenesis.
source: In contrast, newly emerged bees, which are not capable of heat production (Harrison, 1987; Stabentheiner et al., 2010), have significant lower flight muscle octopamine concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harrison, 1987 and Stabentheiner et al., 2010.

claim: AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2 are the predominant octopamine receptor genes expressed in the flight muscle.
source: We determined AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2 as the predominant octopamine receptor genes expressed in the flight muscle, and their expression is detectable across age.
evidence: This is based on the PCR and qPCR data.

claim: The relative expression of AmOARα1 and AmOARβ2 is higher in older bees.
source: The relative expression of both genes is higher in older bees, but at the same time a huge inter-individual variation is detectable.
evidence: This is based on the qPCR data.

claim: Reserpine makes octopamine no longer usable at the flight muscle.
source: Our reserpine experiments solve this problem, because it makes octopamine no longer usable at the flight muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the reserpine mechanism and the experimental results.

claim: Mianserin is a potent octopamine receptor antagonist.
source: This interpretation is supported by the fact that the potent octopamine receptor antagonist mianserin (Grohmann et al., 2003; Balfanz et al., 2014; Blenau et al., 2020) causes hypothermia, too.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grohmann et al., 2003; Balfanz et al., 2014; Blenau et al., 2020.

claim: At least one β octopamine receptor subtype mediates the octopamine signal in the service of thermogenesis.
source: Moreover, our cAMP quantification result suggests that at least one β octopamine receptor subtype mediates the octopamine signal in the service of thermogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the cAMP quantification data.

claim: mAC activation leads to exclusive cAMP increase.
source: Hasan et al., 2014 could show that mAC activation leads to exclusive cAMP increase.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hasan et al., 2014.

claim: β octopamine receptor activation is necessary for honeybee thermogenesis.
source: Our results strongly suggests that β octopamine receptor activation is necessary for honeybee thermogenesis, since these receptors are known to be positively coupled mACs (Balfanz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and the citation to Balfanz et al., 2014.

claim: Alprenolol is active at both β1 and β2 adrenoceptors.
source: This antagonist is active at both, β1 and β2 adrenoceptors (Åblad et al., 1973; Åblad et al., 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Åblad et al., 1973 and Åblad et al., 1972.

claim: Alprenolol represents a putative antagonist of AmOARβ1 and AmOARβ2.
source: Therefore, it represents a putative antagonist of AmOARβ1 and AmOARβ2 and was already used in insects in other studies (Belzunces et al., 1996; Cossío-Bayúgar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between adrenoceptors and octopamine receptors, supported by citations to Belzunces et al., 1996 and Cossío-Bayúgar et al., 2012.

claim: Carvedilol antagonizes preferably α1 and β1 adrenoceptors.
source: Carvedilol antagonizes preferably α1 and β1 adrenoceptors (Hansson and Himmelmann, 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hansson and Himmelmann, 1998.

claim: Yohimbine does not antagonize honeybee β octopamine receptors.
source: Combining the information stated above with our results that alprenolol causes hypothermia but not yohimbine, which does not antagonize honeybee β octopamine receptors (Balfanz et al., 2014; Kovac et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balfanz et al., 2014 and Kovac et al., 2009.

claim: AmOARβ2 is predominantly expressed in the flight muscles when compared with AmOARβ1 and AmOARβ3/4.
source: Since AmOARβ2 is predominantly expressed in the flight muscles (when compared with AmOARβ1 and AmOARβ3/4), AmOARβ2 is the most promising candidate.
evidence: This is based on the PCR data.

claim: AmOARα1 is not in the service of thermogenesis.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that this receptor is not in the service of thermogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of yohimbine on thermogenesis.

claim: Tyramine is capable to reverse the reserpine induced hypothermia.
source: Tyramine is also capable to reverse the reserpine induced hypothermia.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: Tyramine is able to activate octopamine receptors.
source: Based on our results and the fact that tyramine is able to activate octopamine receptors (Grohmann et al., 2003; Balfanz et al., 2014; Blenau et al., 2020), we classify this tyramine effect as artificial and physiologically not relevant.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grohmann et al., 2003; Balfanz et al., 2014; Blenau et al., 2020.

claim: Octopamine acts directly at the indirect flight muscles via the activation of β octopamine receptors.
source: Most likely, this monoamine acts directly at the indirect flight muscles via the activation of β octopamine receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: PKA is in service of thermogenesis.
source: That PKA is in service of thermogenesis is supported by our experiments in which bees are hypothermic as a result of PKA inhibition.
evidence: This is based on the Rp-8-CPT-cAMPS experiments.

claim: PKA might phosphorylate and activate phosphofructokinase 2 (PFK-2).
source: PKA in turn might phosphorylates and activates phosphofructokinase 2 (PFK-2), which is the enzyme that produces fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6P2, Rider et al., 2004).
evidence: This is speculative, supported by a citation to Rider et al., 2004.

claim: F2,6P2 is an activity increasing modulator of phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK-1).
source: F2,6P2 is an activity increasing modulator of phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK-1, Hue and Rider, 1987; Bartrons et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hue and Rider, 1987 and Bartrons et al., 2018.

claim: The PFK-1 mediated phosphorylation of fructose-6-phosphate (F6P) to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (F1,6P2) is a key step in glycolysis.
source: The PFK-1 mediated phosphorylation of fructose-6-phosphate (F6P) to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (F1,6P2) is a key step in glycolysis, at its end ATP is provided (Fothergill-Gilmore and Michels, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fothergill-Gilmore and Michels, 1993.

claim: Heat is generated by the hydrolysis of ATP at the actomyosin complex.
source: Finally, heat is generated by the hydrolysis of ATP at the actomyosin complex (Zhang and Feng, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang and Feng, 2016.

claim: F2,6P2 levels increase in locust flight muscles due to octopamine stimulation.
source: F2,6P2 levels increase in locust flight muscles due to octopamine stimulation (Blau and Wegener, 1994; Blau et al., 1994) and by this controls the rate of carbohydrate oxidation in flight muscles (Wegener, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blau and Wegener, 1994; Blau et al., 1994; Wegener, 1996.

claim: Adrenaline stimulates increasing F2,6P2 levels and thus glycolysis in mammals.
source: In mammals, adrenaline stimulates increasing F2,6P2 levels and thus glycolysis (Narabayashi et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Narabayashi et al., 1985.

claim: Adrenaline's effect on F2,6P2 is achieved by β adrenoreceptor activation followed by stimulation of PKA.
source: This effect is achieved by β adrenoreceptor activation followed by stimulation of PKA (Rider et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rider et al., 2004.

claim: Chronic exercise causes stereotypical adaptations in several tissues of Drosophila melanogaster, which requires the activation of octopaminergic neurons.
source: Chronic exercise causes stereotypical adaptations in several tissues of Drosophila melanogaster, which requires the activation of octopaminergic neurons (Sujkowski et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sujkowski et al., 2017.

claim: In Drosophila muscles, chronic exercise effects are dependent on the activation of β octopamine receptors.
source: In muscles, those effects are dependent on the activation of β octopamine receptors (Sujkowski et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sujkowski et al., 2020.

claim: Honeybees and many other bumblebee species have comparable low FbPase activity.
source: Honeybees and many other bumblebee species have comparable low FbPase activity (Newsholme and Crabtree, 1970; Staples et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Newsholme and Crabtree, 1970 and Staples et al., 2004.

claim: FbPase-PFK cycling rates are not sufficient for heat production.
source: and FbPase-PFK cycling rates are not sufficient for heat production (Clark et al., 1973; Kammer and Heinrich, 1978; Newsholme and Crabtree, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clark et al., 1973; Kammer and Heinrich, 1978; Newsholme and Crabtree, 1976.

claim: Octopamine promotes thermogenesis by directly affecting the flight muscles.
source: Moreover, we have tested our hypothesis and we can show that octopamine promotes thermogenesis by directly affecting the flight muscles.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from the study.

claim: β octopamine receptors are crucially involved in honeybee thermogenesis.
source: Moreover, we show that these effects are mediated by β octopamine receptors.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from the study.

claim: β octopamine receptor genes underlie enormous selective pressure due to adaptation to cold climates.
source: The significance of our results is highlighted by the fact the respective receptor genes underlie enormous selective pressure due to adaptation to cold climates.
evidence: This is based on the citation to Wallberg et al., 2017 mentioned earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Octopamine signaling in the service of thermogenesis might be a key strategy to survive in a changing environment.
source: Finally, octopamine signaling in the service of thermogenesis might be a key strategy to survive in a changing environment.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the findings of the study.

claim: Depleting octopamine in the flight muscles induces hypothermia.
source: we were able to induce hypothermia by depleting octopamine in the flight muscles.
evidence: This is based on the reserpine experiments.

claim: Administering octopamine restores the ability to increase body temperature.
source: Additionally, we could restore the ability to increase body temperature by administering octopamine.
evidence: This is based on the octopamine injection experiments.
